title: The Bodensee-Radweg Full Loop

bestPeriod.note: July and August are ridable but the path through Meersburg and Lindau becomes a slow-moving queue by 11:00.

summary: The full 260 km circuit of Lake Constance across Germany, Austria and Switzerland, stitched together with car ferries, lake steamers and regional trains.
hook: The Bodensee-Radweg is the most heavily used long-distance cycle route in Germany, and it earns that traffic. Seven days lets you ride the whole 260 km circuit at a pace that leaves time for the Untersee, the Rhine delta and two of the lake's islands. It is flat, waymarked to an almost absurd standard, and crosses three countries in a single week without a single serious climb.

snapshot.Country: Germany, with Austria and Switzerland on the loop
snapshot.Base(s): Konstanz (3 nights), Friedrichshafen (1), Bregenz (1), Arbon (1), Konstanz (1)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 270 km, +1,300 m cumulative. Asphalt and compacted gravel, almost entirely traffic-free or on marked lanes
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Zürich, then SBB via Winterthur and Kreuzlingen to Konstanz, around 1 h 40
snapshot.Who It Suits: First-time tourers, families with teenagers, and anyone who wants distance without gradient

itinerary.title: Reichenau and the Untersee
itinerary.morning: Collect bikes in Konstanz. Kultur-Rädle, opposite the station on Bahnhofplatz, has rented trekking bikes and e-bikes here for decades and will fit panniers. Radweg-Reisen, headquartered in Konstanz, is the local operator to use if you want the whole week booked with luggage moved hotel to hotel.
itinerary.afternoon: Ride west along the Untersee shore to Reichenau, the island of three Carolingian and Ottonian churches and a UNESCO listing since 2000. The causeway is flat and the market gardens either side supply most of the lake's vegetables. Continue to Allensbach and back.
itinerary.evening: Konstanz old town. The Niederburg lanes behind the Münster are quieter than the harbour, and the walk out to the Imperia statue is worth twenty minutes.
itinerary.dayStats: 45 km · +150 m · asphalt, short gravel on the Reichenau causeway approach.

itinerary.title: Ferry to Meersburg, on to Friedrichshafen
itinerary.morning: The Konstanz–Meersburg car ferry runs around the clock at roughly 15 minute intervals in daytime and takes about 15 minutes. A cyclist with a bike pays approximately €5. It leaves from Staad, 4 km north-east of the centre.
itinerary.afternoon: Meersburg climbs steeply from the harbour, so walk the Steigstrasse rather than fighting it. Then the shore route through Hagnau, Immenstaad and Fischbach to Friedrichshafen, past orchards that supply the lake's Most and Apfelsaft.
itinerary.evening: Friedrichshafen. The Zeppelin Museum in the old Hafenbahnhof holds a full-scale reconstruction of a section of the Hindenburg. It closes at 17:00, so ride briskly.

itinerary.title: Lindau and the Austrian corner
itinerary.morning: East to Langenargen, Kressbronn and Nonnenhorn, the last German villages. This stretch is the quietest asphalt on the north shore.
itinerary.afternoon: Lindau sits on an island connected by a causeway, with the lion and lighthouse at the harbour mouth. Cross into Austria at Bregenz, only 10 km on. The Pfänderbahn cable car carries bikes for a supplement and drops you at 1,064 m for a view down the whole lake.
itinerary.evening: Bregenz. If the Bregenzer Festspiele is running in July or August, the floating stage on the lake is visible from the shore path for free.
itinerary.dayStats: 40 km · +150 m without the Pfänder, asphalt.

itinerary.title: The Rhine delta into Switzerland
itinerary.morning: South out of Bregenz along the Rheindelta, where the Alpenrhein enters the lake. It is a Ramsar wetland and one of central Europe's better bird sites in spring and autumn. Surface here is compacted gravel on dike tops.
itinerary.afternoon: Cross the Swiss border at Sankt Margrethen, then Rorschach and Horn to Arbon. Swiss francs take over; card payment is universal but ATMs dispense CHF only.
itinerary.evening: Arbon. The lakefront lido and the Saurer museum in the old truck works are both small and both quick.
itinerary.dayStats: 42 km · +180 m · asphalt with 8 km of compacted dike gravel.

itinerary.title: Romanshorn, Kreuzlingen, back to Konstanz
itinerary.morning: Arbon to Romanshorn is 8 km. From here the SBB ferry crosses to Friedrichshafen in about 40 minutes if you want to shortcut; otherwise continue west along the Swiss shore.
itinerary.afternoon: Uttwil, Kesswil, Münsterlingen and Kreuzlingen, which runs seamlessly into Konstanz across the border. The frontier is a line on the pavement with a customs post nobody stops at.
itinerary.evening: Back in Konstanz for two nights. Eat in Kreuzlingen if the Swiss franc is kind, in Konstanz if it is not.

itinerary.title: Stein am Rhein and the Seerhein
itinerary.morning: West from Konstanz along the Seerhein through Gottlieben, then the Untersee's Swiss shore to Steckborn and Berlingen. Reeds, fishing huts, very little traffic.
itinerary.afternoon: Stein am Rhein has the most completely painted Renaissance façades on the Rathausplatz of any town on the lake. Return by SBB from Stein am Rhein to Kreuzlingen with a Velo-Tageskarte, roughly CHF 14, self-loading into the marked carriage.
itinerary.evening: Konstanz. The Sea Life aquarium and the Bodensee-Naturmuseum share a building if the weather has broken.
itinerary.dayStats: 45 km ridden · +200 m · asphalt, short gravel through the Wollmatinger Ried.

itinerary.title: Mainau and the Bodanrück
itinerary.morning: North from Konstanz along the Überlinger See to Mainau, the island garden run by the Bernadotte family. Bikes park at the bridge; the island is walked, not ridden.
itinerary.afternoon: Climb over the Bodanrück ridge through Dettingen and Wallhausen, the only real gradient of the week at around 180 m, then drop back to Konstanz. Return bikes, or continue by train.
itinerary.evening: SBB to Zürich airport takes just under two hours with a change at Winterthur.
itinerary.dayStats: 45 km · +260 m · asphalt with a short forest gravel descent.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Barbarossa
accommodationStrategy.description: A 15th-century house on Obermarkt in the pedestrian core, five minutes from the station and the ferry buses. It has a locked internal bike room, which is the deciding factor in a town where bike theft at the harbour is a genuine problem. Ask for a courtyard room; the square is loud until midnight.
accommodationStrategy.booking: two months ahead, four for June.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Buchhorner Hof
accommodationStrategy.description: A long-established family house two streets back from the harbour, ADFC Bett+Bike certified, with a lockable garage and a hose for washing the bikes down after the delta gravel. Walking distance to the Zeppelin Museum and the ferry pier.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Weisses Kreuz
accommodationStrategy.description: Central Bregenz, close to the Pfänderbahn valley station and the lakefront path, with secure bike storage. It is the practical overnight for the Austrian night because it removes any transfer at the start of the delta ride.
accommodationStrategy.booking: three months ahead if the Festspiele is on.

logistics.emergency: Emergency number is 112 in all three countries. Swiss mountain and lake rescue is reached on 1414 (Rega). Water rescue on the lake is coordinated by the DLRG and the Wasserschutzpolizei.

other.text: Emergency number is 112 in all three countries. Swiss mountain and lake rescue is reached on 1414 (Rega). Water rescue on the lake is coordinated by the DLRG and the Wasserschutzpolizei.

Bike carriage: on German regional trains you need a Fahrradkarte, roughly €6–€7 for a day in Baden-Württemberg. On IC and EC services a bike reservation is compulsory and costs around €9. Swiss trains need a Velo-Tageskarte at roughly CHF 14, with a compulsory reservation on some IC services. Austrian ÖBB regional bike tickets are a few euros. Buy before boarding; conductors fine.
The Katamaran between Konstanz and Friedrichshafen crosses in 50 minutes but carries only a handful of bikes and they must be booked. The Konstanz–Meersburg car ferry has no such limit.
Look for the ADFC Bett+Bike sign. Certified places guarantee a locked bike store, a drying room and a one-night booking.
Three countries, two currencies. Switzerland uses CHF and Austria and Germany use EUR, but Swiss lakeside businesses generally take euro cash at a poor rate. Cards are better.
German shops close at 20:00 and all day Sunday. Swiss shops close at 18:30 on weekdays. Plan food on Saturday afternoon.
Swimming is permitted almost everywhere on the lake, but the Rheindelta reserve has marked no-entry zones during nesting season from March to July.

proTips: Ride the loop clockwise. The prevailing wind is westerly, so a clockwise circuit puts it behind you on the long north-shore day and keeps the lake on your right for photographs.
The Bodensee Card PLUS covers around 160 attractions and both Mainau and the Pfänderbahn. If you use three of them in the week it pays for itself; if you use two it does not.
Take the 07:00 Konstanz–Meersburg ferry rather than a mid-morning one. The path through Meersburg is empty before 09:00 and unusable by noon.

The Bodensee-Radweg splits into a shore variant and an inland variant on several sections. The inland variant is quieter and often shorter; the shore variant has the views. Ride inland when it is busy.

Sailing on the lake works to a Bft scale posted at every harbour. The orange flashing beacons mean a strong-wind warning and boat services stop; that is also your cue that the exposed dike sections will be brutal.
On Mainau, arrive after 16:00. The coach parties leave, the entry queue disappears, and the light on the Italian rose garden is better.
Buy Swiss provisions in Kreuzlingen only if you must. Crossing back into Konstanz for a supermarket saves roughly a third.

packingNotes: 35–40 mm tyres. The dike gravel through the Rheindelta and the Wollmatinger Ried is loose in places.
A dry bag. Lake squalls arrive in under twenty minutes and the exposed shore has no cover.
Swimming kit and a quick-dry towel, carried on top. There are public lidos at Konstanz, Arbon, Lindau and Bregenz.
A cable lock plus a second small lock for wheels; bike theft at ferry piers is common.
Coins in both EUR and CHF for lido lockers and toilets.
Sunglasses and lip balm; glare off the water is constant even in October.
Lights, mandatory in Germany and Switzerland and needed in the Lindau causeway underpasses.
Passport or national ID. Border checks are rare but the Swiss and Austrian frontiers do run spot checks.
whatCouldGoWrong: **High water.** Snowmelt in June can flood shore sections near Radolfzell and the Rheindelta. Signed inland diversions exist; follow them rather than pushing through.

**A ferry cancellation.** Strong wind stops the passenger boats and the Katamaran, though the Konstanz–Meersburg car ferry usually keeps running. Fall back on the train around the lake via Radolfzell and Singen.
**Trains full of bikes.** Summer weekends fill the regional bike carriages by 09:00. Ride the first service of the day or accept the next one.
**Crowding.** In July the path between Meersburg and Friedrichshafen is genuinely dangerous at midday. Ride the inland variant or start at dawn.
**Currency surprises.** Swiss restaurants are 30–50 per cent dearer than German ones. Budget the Arbon night accordingly or eat a picnic on the lakefront.
